power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Psychological processes are characterized by constant change and complex underlying dynamics and are often researched using intensive longitudinal data (ILD).

Although such data are often analyzed with parametric models, these models impose strong and simplified assumptions about the system's dynamic rules that can be unrealistic and may fail to capture phenomena such as multistability.
Recent work has enabled estimation of the stability landscape of psychological systems from ILD, yet drawing statistical inferences from such landscapes remains challenging.
In this work, we present a new method for statistical inference based on stability landscapes.

The core of the method is bootstrapping, complemented by specialized techniques applied before and after the bootstrap procedure to make computation feasible and to effectively summarize information across bootstrap samples.

Across three simulation studies with different data-generating mechanisms, we evaluated the method and, in particular, four approaches for summarizing information about the locations and depths of local minima.
Overall, we found that using fixed reference points, such as the local minima from the original sample, helps guide the assignment of bootstrapped minima.
When the data-generating mechanism differs from the estimated stability landscape, directional bias may occur; however, the relative locations of minima can still be retrieved.
The method generally shows higher precision, whereas achieving high recall may require clear separation between minima, longer time series, and lower measurement noise.
We also provide an empirical illustration using an existing dataset.
An implementation is available in the latest version of the R package fitlandr.
How do we describe the dynamic property of psychological systems?
For a long time, the major approach has been to use parametric models with parameters that are used to give information about questions of interest.
The vector autoregressive model (Bringmann et al., 2013; Hamilton, 1994), for example, uses specific parameters to describe the relationship between one variable and another.
text.formatted: The vector autoregressive model <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bringmann et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Hamilton, 1994)</ref>, for example, uses specific parameters to describe the relationship between one variable and another.

text.text: We can estimate these parameters and their uncertainty levels, and compare them to zero to know if the effect from one variable to another is positive or negative; we can compare them across participants to know whether this effect is stronger for one person than another.
Yet, the assumptions implied by these parametric models are often unrealistic, as psychological systems operate in a far more complex way than the models assume.
Recent developments from the complex systems perspective have pointed to the possibility of an alternative approach (Hayes & Andrews, 2020; Olthof et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Recent developments from the complex systems perspective have pointed to the possibility of an alternative approach <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Hayes & Andrews, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Olthof et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: From this perspective, complex, nonlinear interactions across different elements at all levels give rise to certain psychological phases that differ qualitatively and have important meanings.

These phases may represent, for example, different behavioral patterns that differ in health or sustainability (Heino et al., 2022; Schüler et al., 2025), adaptive and pathological phases in psychopathology (Hayes & Andrews, 2020; Olthof et al., 2023), or the optimal and suboptimal solutions in problem solving (Tulver et al., 2025).

text.text: There, what is in the spotlight is not how strongly one variable is related to another one in time, but rather what states of the system are overall more stable, and whether the psychological system may transition from one phase to another (see Figure 1).

text.text: A key challenge is that researchers often cannot start from the microscopic level and fully understand all dynamics in detail, and similarly, they often cannot specify in advance the functional form of stability across different states.

For example, if we want to know the relationship between the stability of the state and its corresponding depression symptom score, it is very hard to specify the functional form (e.g., quadratic or linear) in advance.
The relationship between stability and mental states can vary substantially across contexts and individuals.
Ideally, we would therefore infer stability directly from the data rather than impose a particular parametric specification.
Illustration of the stability concept for mental states using the ball-and-landscape metaphor.
The theoretical development calls for quantitative methods that can be used in analysis to obtain such a stability landscape from psychological data.

Applying results from applied mathematics, biology, and economics, our recent work has made this possible (Cui, Hasselman, & Lichtwarck-Aschoff, 2026; Cui, Lunansky, et al., 2026; Cui et al., 2023), and subsequent work has shown the potential of this approach to connect and form a uniform bridge between different disciplines and better understand the dynamic properties of a psychological system through various models (Hoekstra et al., 2026; van Bork et al., 2024).

text.text: However, a critical challenge of these recently developed nonparametric methods is the ability to draw statistical inferences.
This is an underdeveloped aspect of the current method.
In fields such as chemistry or biology, there is often less need for statistical inference because of the abundance of data (e.g., Qiu et al., 2022; Zhou & Li, 2016).
text.formatted: In fields such as chemistry or biology, there is often less need for statistical inference because of the abundance of data (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Qiu et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Zhou & Li, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: However, as psychological time series are often limited in length and often contain strong noise, we cannot simply believe the landscape calculated from a data set is accurate at every point.

Instead, we need to know how accurate the estimation is, or in other words, to what extent we can believe the landscape shape and the basins we found are likely to come from actual dynamics of the psychological systems, instead of representing random fluctuations.
Essentially, this issue is comparable to the need for a standard error estimate for an estimated parameter.
When we want to know whether a psychological therapy is effective, for example, we do not only need the mean difference in symptoms before and after treatment.
We also want to know whether this mean difference is significantly different from zero, so we can be confident that the non-zero change is real rather than just random fluctuation.
What motivates us to estimate the error in our landscape estimates is similar.
However, the key methodological challenge presented here is that the target of estimation is not a single value, but rather a landscape surface defined on a two-dimensional state space.
Therefore, a novel methodological workflow is required to make the range estimates and statistical inferences possible.
In the current article, we present a method to draw statistical inferences about estimated landscapes.
It is centered around a nonparametric bootstrapping approach, with specific preparations and an analysis workflow afterward to summarize the results.
We structure the article in the following way.
First, we detail the challenges required for statistical inferences on stability landscapes and the technical solutions we propose.
For certain steps, we propose several possible options and introduce their pros and cons, as well as the considerations behind them.
Second, we use a systematic simulation study to evaluate the method we propose.
Finally, we use an empirical example to showcase the possibility of applying this method in a real-life setting.

On a personal computer, it takes around 10 minutes to give a reasonable accuracy, and may take even longer if a higher accuracy is needed.
This becomes computationally heavy when combined with bootstrapping.
Therefore, the first step to build an inference workflow on stability landscapes is to improve the efficiency for a single estimate.
In fitlandr 0.2, we no longer use the Monte-Carlo simulation for estimating the steady-state distribution.
Instead, we apply a numerical method to directly calculate the steady-state distribution from the drift-diffusion equation.
Specifically, we apply a finite-volume method (FVM; Eymard et al., 2000), illustrated in Figure 2.
text.formatted: Specifically, we apply a finite-volume method (FVM; <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Eymard et al., 2000)</ref>, illustrated in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">2</ref>.

text.text: The central aim of this approach is to find a solution of the probability density p that meets the steady-state criterion: the probability density does not further change over time.
Here, by way of metaphor, it may help to think of the probability as sand in a big box.
We then want to understand how the sand will be distributed in the end if wind blows through the box (representing the dynamic functions).
To achieve this, we try to obtain a simplified local linear representation of how the probability density changes as a function of p.
In the first step (Figure 2a), we divide a finite computational region of the state space into n × n grid of cells (n defaults to 100 in fitlandr).
text.formatted: In the first step (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">2a</ref>), we divide a finite computational region of the state space into n × n grid of cells (n defaults to 100 in fitlandr).

text.text: At the center of each cell, we evaluate the estimated drift and diffusion functions, µ and a.

We then approximate the net probability flow across the four faces shared with orthogonally adjacent cells, meaning how much of the probability flows in and out of the boundaries, as a function of the probability densities in these cells and the estimated drift and diffusion coefficients (Figure 2b).
text.formatted: We then approximate the net probability flow across the four faces shared with orthogonally adjacent cells, meaning how much of the probability flows in and out of the boundaries, as a function of the probability densities in these cells and the estimated drift and diffusion coefficients (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">2b</ref>).

text.text: We impose reflective boundary conditions, so that probability cannot flow out of the computational region.
This is to make sure the sum of probability does not change over time: once the probability flow hits the boundary, it should return back.
In this sand-and-box metaphor, this means we have walls for the box so that no sand can be blown out of the box.
The steady-state probability density vector p can then be estimated by solving Lp = 0 (Figure 2c), subject to the constraint that the density integrates to 1.

text.text: The elements of the sparse n 2 × n 2 matrix L are known and can be calculated based on the estimated diffusion equation and the grid discretization.
Intuitively, this matrix describes how probability flows between neighboring cells.

The exact calculation of these flows is provided in Appendix A. With this numerical approach, the computation time for each run is reduced to seconds, roughly 80 times faster than the previous Monte Carlo approach.
The location and depth of local minima are the primary focus of the inference step, as they contain information on the characteristics of psychological phases and their stability.
A minimum is defined when the value of the potential function at this location, U (x), is lower than all its neighbors.
As we use a rectangular grid for numerical calculations, there are eight neighboring states for each given state.
The potential values outside the estimation boundary are defined as infinite.
After locating all minima, we first need to remove those minima that do not have practical significance or are mainly caused by numerical instability (we call these minor minima).
We apply several rules to label minor minima.
First, we remove the minima that fall outside the convex hull of all the observed data points.
The convex hull of a set of points is the smallest convex polygon that encloses all the points (see Figure 3).
text.formatted: The convex hull of a set of points is the smallest convex polygon that encloses all the points (see Figure <ref type="figure">3</ref>).

text.text: We exclude the outer minima because the actual state of the system has never visited the area outside of the convex hull.
Therefore, the outer region has almost no chance of containing a true minimum informed by data.
At the same time, there is relatively little information regarding the stability of the system.
Therefore, the local minima outside the convex hull are almost certainly due to numerical instability, which is often observed in estimated landscapes.
Illustration of the convex hull for a set of points.
Second, we exclude the basins that are too shallow to be practically meaningful.
The depth of a minimum needs to be defined as the barrier height separating the minimum and another local minimum.
Therefore, we first calculate the minimal energy path between each pair of minima and obtain the barrier height from both sides.

If there is more than one dimension, there are infinite routes connecting two minima, so we first need to find the minimal energy path (MEP), defined as the path that goes through the lowest saddle point between the minima (the detailed algorithm is described in Cui, Olthof, et al., 2026, also see Figure 4a).

text.text: Next, across the landscape, we find the deepest barrier height and the shallowest barrier height.

If the height of the shallowest barrier is lower than 10% of the highest one, we mark this local minimum related to the shallowest barrier as minor, and repeat the procedure again with the remaining minima until the shallowest barrier is at least 10% of the highest one.
We also remove the minima associated with barriers that are shallower than 1% of U max -U min within the convex hull of all observed data points.
This step is to prevent the situation where there is only one flat basin, but some numerical fluctuations exist around the bottom of the basin, resulting in many tiny minima.
In this way, the local minima caused by small local fluctuations can be effectively removed.

Approach 3: Clustering the Locations of Minima.
As both approaches above rely on several fixed minima locations for matching, these fixed points already determine the possible number of minima in the output.

In other words, if the number of fixed points is incorrect, even if other bootstrap samples provide supplementary information supporting the existence of another minimum, it cannot be included in the final output.
Therefore, we also want to explore the approaches that do not use fixed points a priori, but discover them from all bootstrapped minima.
In Approach 3, we perform clustering on all the bootstrap samples and use the mean and covariance of all the minima within a cluster to estimate the minima and their uncertainty.

Specifically, we apply the Hierarchical Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (HDBSCAN, Campello et al., 2013), which is an unsupervised machine learning algorithm that can find clusters of data points.

text.text: It is implemented in the R package DBSCAN (Hahsler et al., 2019).

text.text: The advantages of HDBSCAN, compared to other algorithms, are that it contains relatively few hyperparameters, is robust to hyperparameter selection, and can also identify clusters that are not normally distributed.
Therefore, it is suitable for fitlandr, where the basins may have different shapes and few rules are available for parameter selection.
HDBSCAN can also identify outliers that do not belong to any clusters.
We set the minimum cluster size to 5 points, so that HDBSCAN does not identify clusters containing fewer than 5 bootstrap minima.
For each cluster, we retain at most one minimum per bootstrap sample, choosing the one closest to the provisional cluster center.
This avoids overrepresenting bootstrap samples with multiple minima assigned to the same cluster.
Let the clustering results of HDBSCAN on M boot be {C k } K k=1 , where C k is a set containing the locations of the minima assigned to the k-th cluster, and K is the number of clusters found.
For each cluster, we take the mean location and potential value of the minima (i.e., the centroid of the cluster) as the estimate, and use their covariance as the uncertainty measure:

text.text: Bootstrapping Samples.
There is a potential issue with clustering on all bootstrap minima: it does not take into account the hierarchical structure of the data, namely, minima belong to different bootstrap samples.
This can be problematic when the bootstrap minima do not show clear clusters when taken together, but each of the bootstrap samples still shows consistent patterns (e.g., Figure 6).
text.formatted: This can be problematic when the bootstrap minima do not show clear clusters when taken together, but each of the bootstrap samples still shows consistent patterns (e.g., Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">6</ref>).

text.text: To solve this problem, we apply another approach, in which we first conduct a Hungarian matching on each of the total B(B -1)/2 pairs of the bootstrap samples.
We then form a network with each of the bootstrapped minima as nodes.
The weights of the edges between nodes are given by the distances: when the minima are closer, the edge is also stronger.
After that, we apply the Leiden algorithm (Traag et al., 2019), which is an efficient approach to find clusters from the network.
text.formatted: After that, we apply the Leiden algorithm <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Traag et al., 2019)</ref>, which is an efficient approach to find clusters from the network.

text.text: Each cluster represents a minimum.
To limit excessive splitting of bootstrap minima into separate clusters, we set the Leiden resolution parameter to a relatively low default value of 0.01.
Subsequently, we calculate the locations, depths, and uncertainty of locations for all minima using the same approach as in Approach 3 (Equations 15 and 16).
In this way, we take into account the hierarchical structure of the data, namely, the minima are nested in bootstrap samples.

In all studies, we focus primarily on two key performance indicators.
First, whether the fitlandr method can recover the correct number of minima.
Second, how accurate the location estimated by fitlandr is.

This contains two aspects: precision (among the 95% confidence ellipses of the estimated minima, how many contain the true minima) and recall (among the true minima, how many are covered by the 95% confidence ellipses of the estimated minima).
For evaluating precision and recall, we first use Hungarian matching between the confidence-ellipse centers and the true minima locations.
A true minimum is counted as covered only if it lies within the ellipse matched to it.
Therefore, an ellipse containing two or more true minima can contribute at most one correct match, and each true minimum can also be counted at most once.
In addition, for Simulation Study 1, we examine whether the bootstrapped estimate of ∆U between two minima (i.e., the height difference of the basins) recovers the true values.
The 95% confidence interval for ∆U is given by the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the paired potential differences across bootstrap samples in which both selected minima are represented.
We only conduct this examination when each of the two true minima is contained in exactly one confidence ellipse, and those ellipses belong to different estimated minima.
If the locations of the minima are not correctly identified, we omit this replication for the examination of ∆U.

text.text: The compensation is done per condition and per method.
For each combination of condition and method, we first apply a Hungarian matching for the true minima location and the estimated minima location (per replication).

Note that, although the compensated minima are not at the exact location as the true minima, they still retain the same geographical relationship, and the distance of the compensated minima and true minima are very close compared to the distance of two minima.

text.text: Overall, when there are two minima, it is only feasible to discover two minima with a high success rate when the time series is not too short (with a length of 100 or more), and the minima are well-separated (d = 10).

When the minima are not well separated (d = 5), there is a higher chance of recovering bistability when the time series is longer and the noise is weaker, but overall, the algorithm is more likely to report only one minimum.
When there are three minima, recovering all of them becomes even harder, and there is only a higher success rate when the minima are well separated (d = 10) and the time series is long (T = 500).
We found an additional source of bias in Simulation Study 2, namely that the fitlandr model is misspecified in relation to the MS-VAR model that we simulate from.
The fitlandr method assumes the whole dynamics is only a function of the current state of the system and does not assume an underlying "switch" that controls which dynamics are under operation.
Switching between regimes can induce a systematic bias.

If the system's state is near the minimum of Regime A at one time point but switches to Regime B at the next time point, this creates a strong displacement vector x i+1 -x i from the minimum of Regime A toward the minimum of Regime B. Such a vector interferes with estimating the dynamics around the minimum of Regime A because one expects only small displacement vectors in this region.
The only way to accommodate this contradictory information is shifting the estimated location of Regime A's minimum toward the minimum of Regime B and thus creating a bias.

The level of bias is stronger in Simulation Study 2 than in Simulation Study 1, which means the location from the compensated minima and true minima are larger, but the relative geometric locations are still preserved.

text.text: The current study presents a novel approach to draw statistical inferences on stability landscapes of psychological systems.
This approach relies on bootstrapping applied to the stability landscape.

To make the bootstrapping inference possible, we provided a set of technical solutions, including cross-validation to find the optimal bandwidth, the finite volume approach for precise and efficient calculation, and four approaches to summarize the local minima from bootstrapped landscapes.

To our knowledge, this is the first work to achieve statistical inferences on a potential landscape function from intensive longitudinal data.

Earlier work in other fields that constructs a stability landscape from empirical data, for example, biology (Qiu et al., 2022) and animal movement (Brillinger et al., 2012), typically involved far longer datasets with more precise measurements, where the uncertainty issue is less pressing.

text.text: In psychology, self-reported data from experience sampling are often much shorter and involve larger measurement errors, thus requiring a systematic method to evaluate whether the stability landscape, especially the number and location of basins on it, is obtained with confidence or is more likely to result from random noise.
Nevertheless, we believe the application of the current method is not confined to the field of psychology and experience sampling data.
For any other fields where stability and uncertainty are central focuses, the current method could be potentially applied.

The simulation results showed that, overall, summarizing approaches guided by minima from the full-sample results (Approach 1 and Approach 2) perform better than approaches that directly cluster all bootstrapped minima (Approach 3 and Approach 4).

Although the guidance-free clustering approaches are designed to go beyond the full-sample results and incorporate additional information (Table 1), their performance is unsatisfactory, mainly because they report too many minima.

Further, the performance of fitlandr 0.2 depends on both the data generation mechanism and the specific indicator of interest.
As a non-parametric method that is agnostic about the true data-generation mechanism, we observe some estimation bias in the location of the minima across all simulation conditions.
Consequently, the estimated minima and their associated uncertainty regions may not overlap with the true minima.
In Simulation Study 1, the bias is small and practically unimportant, but it can still affect precision when the time series is long, leading to a small confidence ellipse.
In Simulation Studies 2 and 3, the bias can be larger in some conditions.
In Appendix B, we showed that the main sources of bias include the time gap between observations and the kernel smoothing.

Because the algorithm does not know the data-generation mechanism, it cannot know the true form of the conditional distribution of the next observation given the current one, and therefore has to assume that the first and second moments provide enough information.
Also, because the datasets are not very long, it has to assume that the dynamics are locally similar, so that information from nearby observations can still be used.
These are good approximations when the sampling frequency is high compared to the underlying dynamics, or when the kernel is not too wide.
In Appendix B, we found that the bias would disappear in Simulation Study 1 as the time gap between assessments and the kernel width approach zero.
However, these conditions are not realistic in real life.

To keep the bias low, it is important to ensure that the assessment frequency is not too low relative to the dynamic process, as also found in earlier research (Cui, Hasselman, & Lichtwarck-Aschoff, 2026).

text.text: The kernel bandwidth is optimized through cross-validation and thus should not be manually reduced, but having more data points and more accurate assessments would also help reduce the bandwidth needed.
Furthermore, when the data-generation mechanism deviates more from what fitlandr assumes, it may induce additional bias.
One example is the transient transition behavior caused by regime switching in Simulation Study 2.

When the system is close to Phase A but the underlying mechanism suddenly switches to Phase B, it adds directional, drift-like information around the local minimum of Phase A, making the estimated minimum location lean toward the other phase.

As shown in Appendix B, this bias is intrinsic and results from the mismatch between the assumptions of the data-generating model and the assumptions of fitlandr, rather than from the specific estimation procedure.
Therefore, which model is preferable mainly depends on the theoretical view: whether the true psychological process has a latent "switch", or is better described by a multistable landscape.
Nevertheless, the results of fitlandr still preserve the relative locations of the minima in all simulation studies.

We can see this from the results after compensating for the bias: the confidence ellipses show close to 95% probability of covering the true minimum location when the measurement noise is not too strong.
Meanwhile, the recall rate increases as the time series becomes longer and the minima become more separated.
Therefore, when the psychological phases are sufficiently different and the assessment period is longer, the power of fitlandr to identify minimum locations increases.
While the results for the minima locations showed good performance, the relative depth of the basins is more difficult to estimate.
In Simulation Study 1, although the data generation mechanism aligns well with fitlandr, the estimation of ∆U is biased to zero and has a large confidence interval.
The key reason for this difference is that the information required for minima location estimation is different from basin depth comparison.
Minima location mostly requires local information close to the minima.
However, to obtain the information for depth comparison, we also need information for the region between minima.
In other words, we need to know how exactly the system transitions between minima.

As the minima location represents the most stable psychological states, we naturally have more information there, yet the transition paths need to pass through unstable regions which are relatively rare in data, making the estimation difficult.

In order to better estimate the relative stability of different psychological phases, data with more frequent transitions are probably needed (e.g., data in experimental settings and for phenomena with more frequent changes).
Another possible reason is that we required the system to reside in either basin for at least 25% of the time and discarded time series that did not meet this requirement.
This was mainly intended to ensure that enough data were available to describe each local minimum, but it may have biased the depth estimate.
Overall, in simulation studies, we found that fitlandr leans to the conservative side.
It is more likely to miss true minima or true stability differences, but is less likely to report false minima or differences.
Therefore, it is relatively reliable in empirical settings, even when the time series are short.
The location of the minima is easier to find than their relative depths.

When the true data-generation mechanism differs from what fitlandr assumes, the location of the minima may be biased; the estimated minima may be closer than they actually are, yet the relative location of the minima is still reliable.

In our empirical illustration, the length of the time series is shorter than the adequate values in the simulation studies, yet the result can still show bistability in one case, suggesting the example participant has two psychological phases differing in emotional valence.
However, to improve the statistical power, we still suggest that empirical users collect longer time series to perform analysis with fitlandr.
Future work may also explore other approaches to make use of group information or prior theories to reduce the data length requirement for a single participant.
The key advantage of the current work lies in two parts.
First, fitlandr is a nonparametric approach with few assumptions about the underlying dynamics of the systems.

Without committing to a specific, simplified assumption for the data generation mechanism of psychological data, fitlandr allows various kinds of dynamics to be detected and analyzed in the form of drift-diffusion equations, vector fields, and landscape representations.
In this work, we propose an innovative technical pipeline that shows that drawing inferences from such nonparametric models is technically feasible.
Therefore, it adds an important complement to the toolbox of analysis methods for intensive longitudinal data.
Second, to our knowledge, it is the first method to obtain an estimation of the stability landscape for psychological phases through self-rated time series.

While many theorists have emphasized the use of the stability landscape in understanding complex psychological dynamics, a concrete estimation method was not available until the current line of work, which plays an important role in connecting dynamic systems theories with empirical data and paves the path for future empirical work.

In the earlier version of fitlandr (Cui, Hasselman, & Lichtwarck-Aschoff, 2026), we showed that this pathway is possible, and with the current development, we ground this innovative approach in a solid technical pipeline for statistical inferences, thus making the method practically usable for a wide range of psychological questions and theoretical hypotheses on stability.

For example, it provides the percentage with which a bootstrap minimum occurs in the bootstrap samples, which provides information on how confident we are that a minimum exists.

Incorporating this information and setting a threshold (i.e., only accepting a minimum when it appears in more than a given percentage of bootstrap samples) may also help improve the method's precision.
Nevertheless, as the precision of the method is high in general, the improvement by adding this threshold may be limited unless for more complicated situations.

In simulation studies, we applied a bias-compensation procedure to investigate how much the directional bias influences the precision and recall.
As the data-generating model has certain symmetry properties, the bias should also follow them.

In the λ = 0 conditions of Simulation Study 1 and the two-minima conditions of Simulation Study 2, the actual minima are along the horizontal axis, and both regimes only differ in the equilibrium locations.
Therefore, we expect that when the bias is present, it should be along the horizontal axis as well.

If the bias is inward (i.e., the estimated minima are closer than they actually are), its effect should be the same for both minima, and vice versa (empirically, we found the mean bias is always inward).

Similarly, when the true minima are aligned as vertices of a regular triangle in Simulation Study 2, the bias should point either towards or away from the center of the triangle, and the extent should be the same for all minima.
For the λ ̸ = 0 conditions of Simulation Study 1, the minima are not fully symmetric, but we observe that the empirical bias is similar for both minima.
Also, strictly speaking, the innovation matrix in Simulation Study 2 may break some of the symmetry conditions above.
To make the estimate of bias more stable, we keep these symmetry constraints as an approximation.

Therefore, for Simulation Studies 1 and 2, we (1) calculate all vectors from true minima to the estimated minima from all replications in a given condition, but then (2) only keep the vector component that aligns with the symmetry.

After that, we (3) take the mean of the lengths of all these vectors, and (4) use it to compensate for the bias by shifting the true minima and use these shifted true minima to calculate precision and recall.
